opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question, and I think the difference is less about who's smarter and more about what problem you're trying to solve.

Something like AlphaEvolve is very impressive engineering. You have a strong model proposing code changes, an automated evaluator that scores them, and an evolutionary loop that keeps the good candidates. When you have a clean, verifiable objective, like a faster matrix multiplication kernel or a better scheduling heuristic, that loop works extremely well. A big company also has the compute to run huge numbers of candidates in parallel, so brute-force search becomes a real advantage.

What interests me more is the part that loop doesn't really touch: does the system actually understand *why* something worked, and can that understanding carry over? In most evolutionary setups the model itself stays fixed. The search improves the artifact, but the thing doing the searching doesn't get fundamentally better at searching. To me, recursive self-improvement in the deeper sense means the improvement feeds back into the reasoning process itself, so the next round starts from a better place, not just a better population of programs.

That's also why I care a lot about theory and mechanism. My background is in reinforcement learning, search, and more recently in trying to understand what's happening inside transformers during training: how representations form, why certain reasoning behaviors emerge. If you understand those dynamics, you don't have to rely only on scale to find improvements. You can design the loop so the signal is more efficient, and you need far fewer samples to get somewhere meaningful.

There's a practical side too. If you're not a company with effectively unlimited compute, you can't win by out-searching them. You have to be smarter about where the search happens and what gets learned from it. I actually think that constraint is healthy. It forces you to ask questions about efficiency and generalization that are easy to skip when you can always just throw more GPUs at the problem.

So I'd say they're complementary. The large-lab approach shows what's possible when you have a good verifier and massive compute. What I want to explore is how to make the improvement loop itself more principled, so that self-improvement doesn't just mean "search harder" but actually means "get better at thinking."

r001.rationale: The response discusses large-company compute and the benefits of working under compute constraints, but does not say that a small company has greater organizational focus because self-improvement is its dedicated priority.

r002.rationale: It contrasts AlphaEvolve improving external artifacts such as code while its model stays fixed with Tian’s goal of feeding improvements back into the system’s own reasoning process.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the difference is less about ambition and more about where you put the recursion.

AlphaEvolve is a very impressive system, but structurally it is an evolutionary search wrapped around a frozen model. You have a strong LLM proposing code mutations, an evaluator scoring them, and a population being selected over many generations. The thing that improves is the artifact, whether that is a matrix multiplication kernel or a scheduling heuristic. The model itself doesn't change. The intelligence stays constant and you spend a lot of compute to extract better outputs from it. That works beautifully when you have a crisp, cheap, automatically checkable objective, and Google has both the compute and the infrastructure to run that loop at enormous scale.

What I'm interested in is closing the loop on the model. The question I keep asking is: when the system discovers something, where does that discovery go? In the AlphaEvolve setup it goes into a program, and the next run starts from the same prior. I'd rather the discoveries change the prior. So the data a system generates while solving problems, including the failures and the near-misses, becomes training signal that shifts the weights, and the next round of search starts from a model that has actually learned something. That's what makes it recursive in the real sense rather than just iterative.

Now, that is harder, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. Once you let the model update itself you inherit all the classic problems. Reward hacking becomes much more dangerous because the thing being optimized is also the thing judging. You can collapse diversity and end up with a model that is very confident and very narrow. And you lose the clean separation that makes AlphaEvolve's results so easy to verify. So a lot of my work is actually about the boring parts: how do you build verifiers that the model can't game, how do you keep enough exploration in the loop, how do you know when a self-generated gradient is signal versus noise.

The other difference is practical. I don't have a thousand TPUs to throw at a single kernel. So I care a lot about sample efficiency and about structure. Can the model learn a reusable abstraction from one problem and carry it to the next, instead of rediscovering it through brute force search every time? That's partly a constraint and partly a belief. I think if self-improvement is going to generalize beyond problems with perfect evaluators, it has to run through learning, not just through search.

So I'd say we're complementary. They've shown that search over a strong model can produce real, verifiable discoveries. I'm trying to figure out how to make the model that does the searching get better from doing it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts compute resources and approaches, but does not say a small company has greater organizational focus on self-improvement than a large company treating it as one of many bets.

r002.rationale: It contrasts AlphaEvolve improving external artifacts such as code while its model stays fixed with Tian’s aim of feeding discoveries back into training so the model itself improves.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difference is what part of the system you’re trying to improve. With an approach like AlphaEvolve, you can think of a powerful model proposing changes to an algorithm, and an evaluator checking whether those changes are better. You can get a very effective improvement loop while keeping the underlying model fixed.

The question I’m interested in is whether you can also improve the mechanism that produces those changes. Can the system learn from its attempts so that, in the next round, it becomes better at finding improvements? That’s the recursive part: improving not just the solution, but the ability to improve the solution.

Of course, you have to be careful about what you call progress. Getting better on a particular evaluator doesn’t necessarily mean becoming a better problem solver. So I see these approaches as complementary. A reliable search-and-evaluation loop is an important foundation; the deeper question is how to turn the experience from that loop into a capability that carries over to new problems.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a fixed-model improvement loop with improving the process that generates changes, but does not identify small-company focus versus a large company’s competing bets.

r002.rationale: It describes AlphaEvolve as using a model and evaluator to improve an algorithm, then contrasts that with improving the mechanism that produces changes so the system becomes better at finding improvements.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is what you allow the system to improve. You can have a very powerful search loop where a model proposes code, an evaluator tests it, and the best candidates are retained. But if the model and the search procedure remain fixed, you’re primarily improving the artifact, rather than the mechanism that produces it.

The direction I’m interested in is making that mechanism itself part of the search: can the system improve how it generates hypotheses, designs experiments, and learns from failures? Then the question becomes whether an improvement in one round actually makes the next round more effective.

Of course, you need a reliable evaluation signal. Otherwise, the system can get better at exploiting your metric without getting better at the underlying task. So I see these approaches as complementary. The important question is how much of the improvement loop you can open up while still being able to verify that you’re making real progress.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare small-company focus with large-company competing priorities; it frames the distinction around what the system is allowed to improve.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a fixed model and search procedure improving an artifact with making the mechanism itself part of the search, including improving hypothesis generation, experiment design, and learning from failures.
